newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: AIB consolidates presence in US, buy lauded.
newsitem.headline: AIB consolidates presence in US, buy lauded.

text.p: Allied Irish Bank Plc has underlined its commitment to the United States by buying the Pennsylvania bank Dauphin Deposit Corp in the the biggest acquisition by an Irish company, analysts said.
"It is a very good move," one dealer said. "They got the bank they wanted to buy, they got it at a good price and there is no recourse to shareholders."
AIB announced on Tuesday that it had reached definitive agreement under which its U.S. unit First Maryland Bancorp will acquire Dauphin Deposit Corp for $1.36 billion.
Dauphin, with headquarters in Harrisburg, PA., operates 98 bank branches, through its unit Dauphin Deposit Bank and Trust Co and is deemed a good fit with AIB's other U.S. interests.
"One of the key tenets of AIB's strategy is that they have a desire to have the number one, two or three market share in the areas they are operating in," Davy stockbrokers analyst Emer Lang said.
"Now they are already in York county and they have a sizeable market share there but that really is the strength of their Pennsylvania franchise at the moment," she said.

Dauphin is in 12 counties in Pennsylvania including York "... and that gives AIB good coverage from Baltimore to Harrisburg and it means they will have the number one market share in that area," she said.

This ranks AIB the 45th biggest bank in the U.S. and brings it closer to the size of the smallest of Britain's eight major banks, the Bank of Scotland, which has assets of 45 billion pounds ($74.74 billion).
The move was well received by banking analysts and investors alike.
AIB's share price rose 2.5 percent at 418 Irish pence in early trading on the Dublin stock exchange but later ran into some profit-taking leaving it at 415 Irish pence by midday.

The move was seen underlining AIB's commitment to the U.S. and widening the gap between its portfolio and that of ts main Irish competitor, Bank of Ireland (assets 28 billion punts), who have mirrored each others' moves for years.
Bank of Ireland began to reduce its commitment to the U.S. after a troubled performance by its U.S. unit First Holdings.

In December 1995, Bank of Ireland merged First Holdings with Citizens Financial Group and in April 1996, moved many of its eggs to a UK basket with the acquisition of UK Bristol & West building society, which it bought for 600 million pounds.
"We welcome the fact that AIB and Bank of Ireland are pursuing different strategies because it gives investors a choice. You are no longer comparing like with like," one analyst said.

"We now have two banks who still have very significant home bases growing at a good rate and then if you want an exposure to the mid-Atlantic you opt for AIB and if you want an exposure to UK mortgages you opt for Bank of Ireland."
Lang said she thought AIB's U.S. acquisition was a good fit with the business it already had there.

"We are positive on it. We think that the target Dauphin is a very good fit and the structure of the deal is such that there will be no dilution to earnings so it will have a pretty neutral impact in 1997," she said.
AIB said expects the move to be "moderately accretive" in 1998 and "significantly accretive" in 1999 and beyond.
